notes: Complete administrative court judgment on custody time limit extension and judicial review.

enrichment.short_title: Custody time limit extension upheld despite Crown Court delay in dispatching letter of request
key_facts: Patrick Pierens sought judicial review of HHJ Matheson QC's decision on 13 June 2003 to extend his custody time limit to 25 August 2003.
He was charged with fraudulent evasion of a prohibition on importing cocaine, found at Waterloo on 24 April 2002.
Prolonged delay arose largely from defence requests for letters of request to Dutch and Belgian authorities for witness evidence.
The Crown Court office failed to transmit the Belgian letter of request to the Home Office for about five weeks after 15 April 2003.
The prosecution conceded it had acted with due expedition; the issue was whether there was good and sufficient cause for extension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a Crown Court custody time limit extension decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the judge's extension decision was held not liable to be quashed.
enrichment.ratio: On an application to extend custody time limits under section 22(3) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985, the court may properly consider the entirety of the proceedings when assessing good and sufficient cause, not only the immediate cause of the latest delay; defence-initiated letters of request may constitute good and sufficient cause even where court administration has contributed to delay, provided the decision is within the range open to the judge on review.
legal_issues: Whether good and sufficient cause existed under section 22(3) POA 1985
Whether the judge should have focused only on the immediate pre-application delay caused by the court office
Whether the judge was required to defer or refuse extension for lack of information on the Belgian letter of request

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on Sale of Goods Act implied terms and SAP ratings.

enrichment.short_title: Amptec electric boilers held not in breach of SOGA s14(2) or (3) despite low SAP ratings

statutes_considered.title: Sale and Supply of Goods Act 1994

key_facts: Mr Kelly bought 12 Amptec electric boilers from Jewsons for flats converted at York House, having rejected gas due to cost and delay.
The boilers worked satisfactorially as boilers but were not BRE-coded, causing dramatically lower SAP energy ratings when recalculated.
Low SAP ratings were said to deter purchasers and mortgage lenders, contributing to Kelly's financial collapse and loss of the property.
The deputy judge held Jewsons in breach of implied terms under section 14(2) and (3); Jewsons appealed on those findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from preliminary issue determinations on a counterclaim in proceedings for the price of goods supplied.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Jewsons held not in breach of section 14(2) or (3); permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 14(2) concerns intrinsic satisfactory quality of goods for their ordinary uses, while section 14(3) addresses fitness for a particular purpose communicated to the seller; where a buyer's special purpose (here the effect on SAP ratings and flat marketability) lay within his own expertise and was not communicated for the seller to exercise skill and judgment upon, there is at most partial reliance and no breach of section 14(3), and extrinsic buyer-specific marketability factors are not properly imported into section 14(2).
legal_issues: Overlap between section 14(2) satisfactory quality and section 14(3) fitness for purpose
Whether low SAP ratings rendered boilers unsatisfactory or unfit
Partial reliance and reasonableness of reliance on seller's skill and judgment
Effect of clauses 8.7 and 8.10 of Jewsons' standard terms

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on confidentiality in Children Act proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Overbroad contact-order disclosure ban replaced after father sought to share papers with Families Need Fathers
key_facts: Long-running Manchester County Court contact proceedings concerning AG and her father Mr B, managed by HHJ Hamilton.
Paragraph 3 of the 2 May 2003 order prohibited the father from disclosing court papers to named experts, Families Need Fathers or similar organisations, with a penal notice attached.
The father, a litigant in person, appealed with pro bono representation; CAFCASS Legal Services appointed an advocate to the court.
Families Need Fathers provided written submissions on the support they give members.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted at oral hearing against paragraph 3 of a contact/residence order; wider permission applications dismissed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the narrow disclosure issue; paragraph 3 replaced with a tailored order permitting limited summaries when seeking case advice; other permission applications refused.
enrichment.ratio: Publication under section 12 AJA 1960 and section 97 Children Act 1989 is not confined to formal media promulgation and may include private oral communications depending on circumstances, but additional bespoke restrictions beyond the statutory scheme require precision especially where penal notices attach; a litigant in person may disclose a limited summary of orders, proposed applications, issues and parties' positions when seeking advice, while document disclosure to persons outside Rule 4.23(a)-(e) still requires court leave.
legal_issues: Meaning of publication/publish in sections 12 AJA 1960 and 97 Children Act 1989
Whether paragraph 3 was justified given existing statutory confidentiality
Whether the order was too imprecise to enforce with a penal notice
Whether Rule 4.23 unfairly disadvantages litigants in person

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on Calderbank costs in big-money ancillary relief.

enrichment.short_title: Calderbank costs in ancillary relief: FPR 2.69B workable but reform urgently needed post-White

statutes_considered.title: Family Proceedings (Miscellaneous Amendments) Rules 1999
provisions: SI 1999/1012 applying CPR Part 44 to family proceedings

key_facts: Two conjoined appeals concerned costs orders following Calderbank negotiations in substantial ancillary relief cases (Norris and Haskins).
Bennett J ordered Mr Norris to pay 80% of Mrs Norris's costs; Mr Blair QC ordered Mr Haskins to pay 85% of Mrs Haskins's costs.
Mr Norris applied out of time for permission to appeal, relying on Mr Mostyn QC's later decision in GW v RW.
The court reviewed Gojkovic (No 2), the post-White shift to ascertaining shares in marital assets, and problems after revocation of Rule 2.69C.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals on permission to appeal and extension of time (Norris) and permission to appeal (Haskins), with substantive guidance on costs rules.
enrichment.outcome: Haskins appeal dismissed; Norris application for permission to appeal and extension of time refused.
enrichment.ratio: Costs in ancillary relief must be determined under CPR 44.3 read with FPR 2.69, 2.69B and 2.69D; Rule 2.69B remains workable despite revocation of 2.69C and requires consideration of all offers including counter-offers under Rule 2.69D(a), with broad discretion to depart where unjust; judges may not treat the rules as incomprehensible and substitute a clean-sheet no-order regime, though post-White equality-based distribution and costs assessment culture warrant urgent rule reform.
legal_issues: Proper approach to Calderbank offers and counter-offers under FPR 2.69B and 2.69D
Whether Gojkovic (No 2) starting point survives White v White
Whether Rule 2.69B is incomprehensible after revocation of 2.69C
Whether Norris should be granted extension of time to appeal costs

notes: Complete Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) judgment refusing leave to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Shayler leave refused: OSA trial restrictions fair despite self-representation and witness anonymity
key_facts: David Shayler, a former MI5 officer, was convicted of three Official Secrets Act 1989 offences for disclosing security and intelligence material to the Mail on Sunday.
The House of Lords had ruled public interest was no defence and duress/necessity were excluded.
Shayler chose to represent himself; the Crown sought anonymity for witnesses, advance notice of security-related topics, and limits on credit cross-examination.
Moses J allowed screened anonymous evidence, a notice regime for security/intelligence matters, and restricted credit questions aimed at advancing a forbidden public-interest justification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against conviction after refusal on paper by the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Renewed application for leave to appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Individually justified trial restrictions on an Official Secrets Act prosecution—including anonymous witness screening, a notice regime before raising security/intelligence matters, and limits on credit cross-examination pursuing a excluded public-interest defence—do not cumulatively render the trial unfair or deny equality of arms where a self-represented defendant is treated no more favourably than counsel would have been.
legal_issues: Whether cumulative trial restrictions breached Article 6 fair trial rights
Whether self-representation caused unfair discrimination
Lawfulness of witness anonymity and in camera procedure applications
Whether advance notice requirements and credit rulings were disproportionate

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on share sale agreement preferred supplier rights.

enrichment.short_title: Motorcare share sale: KRA varied preferred supplier rights; 10-mile first refusal upheld
key_facts: Dunblane Property and Mr Rand sold shares in Motorcare Services Ltd (MSL) to Powerstore under a 16 May 1995 share sale agreement with preferred supplier protections in Schedule 3.
Knightsbridge Cars (Bodyshop) Ltd (KBL), a Dunblane subsidiary, sought preferred supplier status for accident repair referrals (ARNs) but MSL failed to honour the 10-mile preference zone.
After disputes, Mr Rand and Mr Vlotman agreed a Key Repairers Agreement (KRA) on 26 March 1996 fixing 40 ARNs per month and specified postcodes.
The judge held the KRA did not affect SSA rights; the Court of Appeal held it varied implementation for Kingsbury from its effective date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from preliminary issue determinations in a breach of share sale agreement claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; paragraph 4 Schedule 3 construed as 10-mile first refusal; KRA held to vary SSA for Kingsbury from effective date but not for past periods or other KBL sites; Iver issue set aside for trial.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 4 of Schedule 3 to the SSA conferred on a metropolitan preferred supplier a right of first refusal over ARNs within a maximum 10-mile road distance from its repair shop; objectively, the March 1996 KRA between MSL and KBL varied the parties' SSA rights for Kingsbury from its effective date, but did not settle past breaches or apply to other KBL premises.
legal_issues: Construction of locality and 10-mile radius in Schedule 3 paragraph 4
Effect of the 21 August 1995 ARA on SSA rights
Whether the March 1996 KRA replaced or merely implemented preferred supplier rights
Whether past disputes were compromised at the 14 March 1996 meeting

notes: Complete High Court judgment on VAT section 80 repayment and unjust enrichment.

enrichment.short_title: Car-leasing VAT repayment refused: manufacturers' bonuses were discounts and unjust enrichment established
key_facts: Lombard (NatWest leasing entity) claimed repayment of about £706,347 VAT overpaid on manufacturers' bonuses treated as taxable supplies before Elida Gibbs.
Following Elida Gibbs, bonuses were correctly treated as purchase-price discounts, inflating blocked input tax on vehicle purchases.
Customs invoked unjust enrichment under section 80(3), arguing Lombard passed the cost to lessees through rentals.
Other leasing companies received repayments without unjust enrichment analysis; the Revenue Adjudicator criticised inconsistent treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from the VAT and Duties Tribunal to the High Court (Chancery).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Tribunal decision reversed; repayment refused on unjust enrichment grounds; unfair treatment point held outside tribunal jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 80(3) VATA the Commissioners bear the burden of proving unjust enrichment; where a lessor incorporated overstated vehicle cost (including wrongly treated VAT on manufacturers' bonuses) into lease pricing in a competitive market, repayment would unjustly enrich the claimant because customers bore the economic cost; unequal treatment of similar taxpayers does not require perpetuating erroneous repayments and is not within the VAT tribunal's jurisdiction under section 83(t) or section 84(10).
legal_issues: Whether Lombard suffered loss or passed on blocked input tax to customers
Burden and standard of proof on unjust enrichment defence
Whether the tribunal erred in finding no unjust enrichment
Whether unequal treatment of Lombard compared with rivals required repayment

notes: Complete CCRC reference appeal; conviction quashed on fresh DNA evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Shirley murder conviction quashed: DNA excluded appellant as semen contributor
key_facts: Michael Shirley was convicted in January 1988 of murdering Linda Cook in Portsmouth in December 1986 after an 11-1 jury verdict.
Original case rested on blood-group semen evidence, injuries, a Flash shoe impression, and a missing half-hour in his movements.
CCRC referral led to LCN DNA profiling showing a male DNA contributor other than Shirley in intimate swabs, with no semen on the victim's knickers.
The Crown accepted safety of conviction required proof to the criminal standard that a second unknown man had earlier intercourse with the victim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following CCRC reference under section 9(1) Criminal Appeal Act 1995 after earlier leave refused in 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh DNA evidence excluding the appellant as contributor to semen in intimate swabs, combined with the absence of semen on the victim's knickers and the implausibility of a second unknown contributor on the facts, rendered the 1988 conviction unsafe notwithstanding remaining circumstantial evidence.
legal_issues: Effect of fresh DNA evidence on the four planks of prosecution evidence
Whether a second unknown male contributor must be established to the criminal standard
Whether circumstantial evidence (injuries, shoe mark, timings) dispelled DNA-based exoneration
Admissibility of late expert evidence from Dr Ford

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment discharging without-notice freezing order.

enrichment.short_title: Without-notice freezing order discharged for lack of dissipation evidence against Tomlinson
key_facts: After a misfeasance judgment against director Knopp, HHJ Thompson made a without-notice freezing order against Mr Tomlinson and Reyall Business Consultants Ltd.
Tomlinson was not present or represented when the order was granted; no application notice or affidavit explaining absence of notice was provided.
The order restrained assets up to £1m (Tomlinson) and £50,000 (Reyall), including three properties later shown not to belong to them.
Neuberger J refused discharge; the Court of Appeal held the order should never have been made on the evidence before the judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from refusal to discharge a without-notice freezing order made after a related trial judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; freezing order discharged; costs to Tomlinson and Reyall.
enrichment.ratio: A without-notice freezing order requires strict compliance with CPR Part 25, including affidavit evidence of a good arguable case, real risk of asset dissipation, and reasons for no notice; dishonesty or adverse findings in related proceedings against a non-party do not substitute for solid evidence of dissipation, and failure to meet these requirements renders the order unjustified.
legal_issues: Whether there was a real risk of dissipation of assets
Procedural compliance on without-notice freezing order applications
Whether findings against Tomlinson in Knopp proceedings could be relied upon
Whether residence in the Isle of Man justified the order

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on demurrage and shifting expenses at Dakar sealine.

enrichment.short_title: Afrapearl demurrage payable after defective Dakar sealine delays; half-rate breakdown rejected
key_facts: Owners chartered Afrapearl to Vitol under an Asbatankvoy voyage charter to discharge fuel oil at Dakar and Gibraltar.
Discharge at the M'bao sealine was delayed by a pre-existing leaking, corroded pipeline damaged since at least 2000.
The vessel berthed, attempted discharge, shifted off twice for repairs, and finally completed using a temporary hose repair.
Charterers argued laytime/demurrage did not run or ran at half rate under clauses 6, 7 and 8; Owners claimed demurrage and shifting expenses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of demurrage and additional agency fees claim; interlocutory refusal of late amendments on time bar and awaiting tide.
enrichment.outcome: Owners succeeded; demurrage of US$455,851.44 and additional agency fees of US$100,007.03 awarded; late time-bar and awaiting-tide amendments refused.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 6 delay-getting-into-berth exception applies only before first berthing after arrival, not to subsequent shifts; clause 7 excludes only initial anchorage-to-berth movement, with post-berthing shifts governed by clause 9; pre-existing sealine damage causing unusability was not a breakdown of consignee equipment under clause 8, so full demurrage ran and shifting costs were recoverable as shifts between berths.
legal_issues: Construction of laytime exceptions in clauses 6, 7 and 8 of the charterparty
Whether sealine leak constituted breakdown of consignee equipment
Recoverability of additional shifting expenses under clause 9
Whether Claims Clause time bar defeated port expense claim
